Alcudia is a port town in the Spanish autonomous territory Balearic Islands. The town covers a total area of approx 60 km2 (23 mi2) and has population around 3,000. The port is located on the northern coast of Majorca Island.

Alcudia is a resort town mainly popular among families. Most of its hotels are in Port d'Alcudia and Platja d'Alcudia along the 14 km (9 mi) long beach stretching to Can Picafort. The well-preserved Old Town is surrounded by a medieval wall and features many houses from the 13th-century. Outside the town walls, there are remains of a Roman town with an amphitheater. North of Alcudia is the 19th-century built bullring (bullfighting arena).

The old town hosts an outdoor market on Sundays and Tuesdays. Inside the town walls are also several popular bistros and restaurants famous for their home-cooked food. Most restaurants in Port Alcudia are around the Marina and most of them are only open during the summer tourist season. Further to the north and west can be found coves and several beaches good for snorkeling, swimming, sunbathing. Alcudia is also well-known for its annual St Jaume Festival, held in early-July for 9 days.

Regularly-scheduled cruiseferries link Alcudia to mainland Spain (Barcelona) and Menorca Island (Ciutadella de Menorca). The company BALEARIA serves the Alcudia-Barcelona route with 15 weekly crossings (travel time ~6 hours) and the Alcudia-Ciutadella route with 4 daily crossings (travel time ~1 hour). A second large ferry company (TRASMEDITERRANEA) serves the Alcudia-Ciutadella route with 12 weekly crossings (~2 hours travel time).

Alcúdia is a good port for independent sightseeing. The medieval old town, Roman remains, Port d'Alcúdia waterfront and a long sandy beach are all close enough for a normal cruise call. More distant sights such as Formentor and s'Albufera are also possible, but require transport and more attention to timing.

At a Glance

  • Independent sightseeing: Easy for Alcúdia Old Town, Pol·lèntia, the port waterfront and Alcúdia Beach.
  • Cruise arrival: Cruise ships may anchor offshore and use tenders. Alcúdia also has a commercial ferry terminal, but it should not be assumed that this will be the cruise passenger exit. Follow the ship's information for the actual landing point.
  • Old Town: From the commercial Estació Marítima area it is roughly 2.5 km (1.6 mi) to the historic centre; a taxi or local bus is more practical than walking if time is limited.
  • Terrain: The port and beach areas are largely flat. The old town has cobbled streets, uneven paving and some steps around the walls.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Alcúdia does not have the predictable cruise-terminal setup found in Palma. Cruise calls are relatively infrequent, and ships can use the anchorage rather than berth alongside the ferry facilities. Tender passengers should therefore check where their ship is landing before planning a walking route.

The commercial passenger terminal, Estació Marítima, is on the Port d'Alcúdia waterfront. In the summer season, TIB bus line 323 serves the maritime station and connects it with Alcúdia town and Alcanada. The main Port d'Alcúdia bus stops have additional routes serving the old town, beaches and other parts of northern Mallorca.

A taxi is the simplest option for the old town and normally avoids spending valuable port time waiting for a bus. Do not assume that a cruise-line shuttle will operate unless your ship specifically announces one.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Alcúdia Old Town and Roman Pol·lèntia

Allow about 2.5–3.5 hours. This is the best all-round choice for a first visit and is easy to arrange independently. Take a taxi or local bus to the historic centre, then explore the medieval gates, narrow streets, Plaça de la Constitució, Sant Jaume Church and sections of the city walls.

The archaeological remains of Roman Pol·lèntia lie immediately south of the medieval centre. The site includes residential remains, the forum area and a Roman theatre, making it easy to combine Roman and medieval Alcúdia without another transfer.

Port d'Alcúdia and Alcúdia Beach

Allow about 2–4 hours. This is the easiest relaxed option, especially when tenders land near the Port d'Alcúdia waterfront. Walk around the marina and waterfront before continuing to the sandy beach.

Alcúdia Beach extends for more than 7 km (4.3 mi) along the bay, with shallow water and a developed resort section near the port. There is no reason for cruise passengers to travel far along the beach unless they specifically want a quieter section.

Alcanada Coast

Allow about 2–3 hours. Alcanada lies east of the commercial port and provides a quieter alternative to the main resort beach. The coast is rocky and pebbly rather than a broad sandy strand, with pine trees and views toward the small island and Alcanada lighthouse.

Seasonal TIB line 323 links the maritime station with Alcanada, or it is a short taxi ride. Walking is also possible for reasonably fit passengers and is most convenient if the ship's landing point is near the commercial port.

S'Albufera de Mallorca Natural Park

Allow about 3–4 hours. This is a worthwhile independent option for birdwatchers and nature enthusiasts. The main entrance at Pont dels Anglesos is around 6 km (3.7 mi) from Alcúdia town and is served by TIB routes along the Alcúdia–Can Picafort corridor.

Visitors enter on foot or by bicycle, and the information centre is about 1 km (0.6 mi) inside the park. A free visitor permit is obtained at the information centre. Because a proper visit involves additional walking to hides and observation areas, this is better for passengers who have at least several hours ashore after allowing for transport.

Formentor Peninsula

Allow about 4–6 hours. Formentor offers one of northern Mallorca's principal scenic excursions, with Port de Pollença, Mirador del Colomer, Formentor Beach and the lighthouse among the possible stops.

Independent travel is possible with seasonal TIB line 334 from Alcúdia, but services and access arrangements should be checked on the day. Road access to the peninsula is regulated during the busy season, and private-vehicle restrictions can apply. For a short cruise call, a ship or organized excursion is usually the safer choice because it removes the risk of waiting for buses or dealing with seasonal traffic controls.

Self-Guided Walking Tours

Easy to Moderate: Alcúdia Old Town and Pol·lèntia

Start: Alcúdia Centre Històric or Pol·lèntia bus stop after transferring from the port.

  1. Enter through Porta de Mallorca and look at the medieval walls and moat.
  2. Follow the old streets toward Plaça de la Constitució.
  3. Continue through the historic centre to Porta del Moll, or Xara Gate.
  4. Walk along the wall perimeter toward Sant Jaume Church.
  5. Visit the nearby Pol·lèntia archaeological area.
  6. If time permits, continue through the Roman site toward the Roman Theatre before returning to the old town bus stop or taxi rank.

Distance: about 2.5 km (1.6 mi), depending on how much of Pol·lèntia is included.
Pure walking time: about 45–55 minutes.
Recommended total time: 2–3 hours with sightseeing stops.
Difficulty: Easy to moderate. Mostly level, but expect cobbles, uneven paving and occasional steps.

Moderate: Port to Alcanada Coastal Walk

Start: Estació Marítima or the eastern side of Port d'Alcúdia.

  1. Leave the passenger-terminal area toward the fishing harbour.
  2. Continue east along the port roads toward Camí d'Alcanada.
  3. Pass the area around Torre Major, the old coastal watchtower.
  4. Continue through the residential area to Cala Poncet.
  5. Finish at Alcanada Beach for views across to the lighthouse island.
  6. Return by the same route, or use seasonal bus line 323 if its timetable suits your ship.

Distance: roughly 5 km (3.1 mi) round trip from the commercial port area.
Pure walking time: about 1 hour 15 minutes.
Recommended total time: 2–3 hours.
Difficulty: Moderate. Mostly easy surfaces with a few inclines, but the route is exposed to the sun and some sections follow roads rather than a continuous seafront promenade.

Practical Tips

  • If the ship is tendering, allow extra time for both the outbound tender and the return queue. The ship's stated last-tender time is more important than the scheduled departure time.
  • For a short call, prioritize the old town and either the Roman site or beach rather than trying to cross Mallorca to Palma.
  • Local buses are useful, but check the current timetable before committing to a longer independent trip such as Formentor or s'Albufera.
  • Summer heat can make even short walks tiring. Carry water and sun protection, particularly around Pol·lèntia, the walls and the Alcanada coast.
  • When travelling beyond Alcúdia, plan to return to the port area well before the ship's required boarding or last-tender time and allow additional margin for road traffic and bus delays.
